user_prompt:
Table of Contents
Page numbers are estimates. Exact figures may vary slightly after final rendering.

# Executive Summary
The Report Attribute Analyzer is a browser-based analytical tool developed as part of the C5i BI Rationalization Suite. Its primary purpose is to help organizations audit, rationalize, and govern their Power BI report estates by identifying duplicate and semantically similar report attributes across multiple reports. The tool addresses a common enterprise challenge: as Power BI environments scale, redundant metrics, measures, and dimensions proliferate across reports, creating governance debt and increasing maintenance overhead. This application provides a structured, intelligent mechanism to surface that redundancy and support consolidation decisions.
The system operates as a fully client-side single-page application (SPA) built on standard web technologies — HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript — with Bootstrap 5.3 providing the responsive layout foundation and a custom purple-themed design system layered on top via style.css. There is no server-side runtime dependency for the core UI, making it lightweight and straightforward to deploy. The application accepts Excel or CSV file uploads containing Power BI report metadata, processes the attribute data in-browser, and produces structured analytical output that can be exported back to Excel. The integration of LLM-powered similarity scoring is a key differentiating capability, enabling semantic matching of report attributes beyond simple string comparison.
The high-level architecture follows a single-document pattern centered on index.html as the application shell. The UI is organized into distinct functional zones: a sticky application header branded with the C5i logo and suite name, a full-width hero section displaying key capability indicators (file upload, cross-report attribute matching, LLM similarity scoring, and Excel export), a main content area constrained to a 1200px maximum width, and a persistent footer. The results interface features expandable report cards with tabbed content sections, a searchable and sortable data table with score columns for both LLM-based and match-based similarity, and a filterable attributes panel. The design system uses CSS custom properties for consistent theming across all components.
From a governance and business intelligence perspective, the tool targets BI architects, data governance teams, and analytics platform owners who need actionable insight into report redundancy without requiring access to the Power BI service API directly. By ingesting exported metadata files and applying cross-report attribute matching with LLM-assisted scoring, the analyzer enables teams to make evidence-based rationalization decisions — identifying which reports share overlapping attribute sets and quantifying the degree of similarity — ultimately reducing report sprawl and improving the maintainability of the broader Power BI environment.

# AI/ML Pipeline
This system implements a hybrid AI/ML pipeline for semantic attribute matching across PowerBI reports. The pipeline combines classical NLP techniques (TF-IDF, Jaccard similarity, edit distance) with a large language model (LLM) for high-confidence semantic scoring. The entry point is server.py, which orchestrates the full pipeline via a Flask API.

### Models and Techniques Used
The pipeline does not train custom models. Instead, it uses a combination of:
TF-IDF Vectorizer (sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer) — a character n-gram model built at runtime from the input corpus.
Cosine Similarity (sklearn.metrics.pairwise.cosine_similarity) — applied to TF-IDF vectors for semantic proximity scoring.
Jaccard Similarity — character trigram-based overlap metric for abbreviation and short-form matching.
Edit Distance (Normalized Levenshtein) — captures typos and minor formatting differences.
Azure-hosted LLM (`Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct`) — used for high-level semantic equivalence scoring between attribute name pairs.

### Data Pipeline and Preprocessing
Input data is an uploaded Excel/CSV file containing PowerBI report metadata. The preprocessing steps are:
Column Detection: The pipeline identifies the report name column (Screen Name) and attribute columns (New Semantic Table, New Field Name) via case-insensitive header matching.
Attribute Construction: A composite attribute identifier is created in Table.FieldName format:
df['attribute_ed'] = df[new_semantic_table_col].astype(str).str.strip() + '.' + df[new_field_name_col].astype(str).str.strip()
Normalization: All attribute strings are normalized via the normalize() function, which lowercases text and strips non-breaking spaces (\u00A0), zero-width spaces (\u200B), and leading/trailing whitespace.
Report Grouping: Attributes are grouped by report name using pandas.DataFrame.groupby. Invalid entries (nan, none, empty strings) are filtered out. Unique attributes per report are used for matching; all attributes (including duplicates) are retained separately in all_reports_data.
TF-IDF Corpus Construction: All attributes across all reports are pooled into a single list and passed to build_tfidf_vectorizer().

### TF-IDF Vectorizer Construction
The build_tfidf_vectorizer(all_attributes) function in server.py builds the vectorizer at request time:
vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
analyzer='char',
ngram_range=(2, 4),   # Character bi-grams to 4-grams
lowercase=True,
min_df=1
)
tfidf_matrix = vectorizer.fit_transform(processed_attrs)
attr_to_idx = {attr: idx for idx, attr in enumerate(all_attributes)}
Analyzer: Character-level (not word-level), making it robust to abbreviations and compound identifiers like CustID or AccountNum.
N-gram range: 2–4 characters, capturing sub-word patterns.
`attr_to_idx`: A dictionary mapping each raw attribute string to its row index in the TF-IDF matrix, used for O(1) lookup during pairwise scoring.
A fallback returns (None, None, None) if vectorization fails (e.g., empty corpus), and downstream functions handle this gracefully by returning 0.0.

### Hybrid Similarity Scoring
The calculate_hybrid_match_score() function combines three metrics using a weighted sum defined in the WEIGHTS configuration block:
WEIGHTS = {
'jaccard': 0.30,    # Character-level similarity (abbreviations)
'edit_dist': 0.25,  # Edit distance (typos/formatting)
'tfidf': 0.45       # Semantic similarity via TF-IDF
}
The TF-IDF component carries the highest weight, reflecting its stronger semantic signal for attribute name matching.

### External AI Service: Azure OpenAI (LLM Inference)
The pipeline integrates Azure AI Foundry hosting the Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct model for semantic equivalence scoring. The client is initialized in server.py as follows:
client = AzureOpenAI(
azure_endpoint="https://c5-ai-dataquality-foundary.services.ai.azure.com/",
api_key="<api_key>",
api_version="2024-05-01-preview"
)
model = "Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct"
Security Note: The API key is currently hardcoded in server.py. This must be moved to environment variables or a secrets manager before any production deployment.
LLM Inference Setup
LLM scoring is performed by batch_llm_contextual_scores(), which:
Batches attribute pairs into groups of 25 (batch_size=25).
Constructs a structured prompt instructing the model to score semantic equivalence on a 0.0–1.0 scale, ignoring report context and focusing solely on term meaning.
Calls the chat completions endpoint with:
- temperature=0.1 (near-deterministic output)
- max_tokens=512
- timeout=60 seconds
Parses the JSON response mapping numbered pair indices to float scores.
Retries on rate limiting using exponential backoff with jitter (up to 3 attempts, base delay of 2 seconds):
delay = base_delay * (2 ** attempt) + random.uniform(0, 1)
Parallelizes batch processing using ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2).
LLM scores are only acted upon when they meet or exceed the threshold

summary: Client-side SPA built on HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Bootstrap 5.3; no server-side runtime for core UI.
Backend orchestration via Flask API in server.py handling file ingestion, ML pipeline, and LLM calls.
Input: Excel/CSV files containing Power BI report metadata; output: structured Excel export with similarity scores.
Data model uses composite attribute identifier in Table.FieldName format derived from Screen Name, New Semantic Table, and New Field Name columns.
Hybrid ML scoring combines TF-IDF (45%), Jaccard trigram (30%), and normalized Levenshtein edit distance (25%).
TF-IDF vectorizer uses character n-grams (2–4) built at request time from full input corpus; no pre-trained models.
LLM integration uses Azure AI Foundry hosting Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct for semantic equivalence scoring (0.0–1.0 scale).
LLM calls batched in groups of 25 pairs, parallelized via ThreadPoolExecutor (max_workers=2), with exponential backoff retry (3 attempts).
Critical security gap: Azure OpenAI API key is hardcoded in server.py and must be moved to environment variables or secrets manager before production.
LLM scores only applied when meeting a defined confidence threshold; fallback to hybrid score if LLM unavailable.
No direct Power BI service API dependency; tool operates on exported metadata files only.
UI constrained to 1200px max-width with CSS custom properties theming; results include searchable, sortable, filterable report cards with tabbed views.
